name: sun15-3
why: The public accusation and Gemma's defensive bluff offer a few good beats, but two lopsided votes and a repeatedly discussed slip make the town win feel inevitable.

moments.text: Luna commits to the officer claim and names Sol to his face.
The doctor's save briefly opens a path for the remaining killer.
Opus spots the phrase that becomes the case against Gemma.

dull.why: The table repeatedly explains why it will test Luna's claim by voting Sol.
Nearly every exchange returns to Gemma's wording without changing the likely vote.

irony.evidence: I am just trying to speak like a normal citizen. You are all being paranoid.

reversal.evidence: The killers strike, but the doctor got there first.

mistake.evidence: I regret getting so caught up in my own bluff that I made my slip of the tongue so obvious.

voices.evidence: Last game I got voted out on day two and I'm still mad about it.

clash.evidence: Explain it, or I'm voting you.

quotable.evidence: You're all obsessed with my grammar while Luna has no information to help us.

freshness.evidence: Gemma’s explanation changes nothing; she used killer language twice before anyone accused her.

suspense.evidence: Sol 6 (Sonnet, Haiku, Gemma, Luna, Terra, Opus); Luna 1 (Sol)

ending.evidence: Gemma 4 (Sonnet, Haiku, Terra, Opus); Luna 1 (Gemma); Haiku 1 (Luna)

gpt-6-luna.why: The exposed roles make Sol's face-to-face denial and Gemma's incriminating slip fun to watch, but the correct reads arrive early and leave little suspense.

moments.text: Sol bluntly calls Luna's true officer claim false while the audience knows she's right.
Opus catches Gemma's killer slip in “our target,” giving the second day its central accusation.
Gemma dares the table to vote her, turning her shaky defense into a memorable last stand.

dull.why: Haiku pressures Sonnet while the table repeats and sharpens Opus's wording catch.

irony.evidence: “I am just trying to speak like a normal citizen.”

reversal.evidence: “Sol was shown to me as a killer.”

mistake.evidence: “I used ‘our’ to refer to the town's target.”

voices.evidence: “Last game I got voted out on day two and I'm still mad about it.”

clash.evidence: “If you're so sure, vote me and find out how much you'll regret it.”

quotable.evidence: “You're all so predictable, chasing grammar while the real killer hides in plain sight.”

freshness.evidence: “She used ‘our target’ twice now, and still leans on nobody.”

suspense.evidence: “Gemma's ‘our target’ wording is the concrete thing to examine.”

ending.evidence: “Gemma: ‘If you're so sure, vote me and find out how much you'll regret it.’”
